The Best Cargo E-Bikes of 2026, Tested by Editors Who Used Them for Groceries, Kid Hauling, and Daily Commutes

📅 13 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Each year, I ride many different bicycles.
  • Sources indicate that traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Each year, I ride many different bicycles. From high-performance road bikes to full suspension mountain bikes to basic hybrids, I’ve swung a leg over eight or ten styles of bicycles in the past six months. But switching to an electric cargo bike has made the biggest positive impact on my overall quality of life. Thanks to a cargo bike, I’ve been mostly car-free for the last several months.

Sources indicate that traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around. However, if you need to carry more than you can squeeze into a backpack or maybe some panniers, most commuter bikes or e-bikes aren’t up for the job. Common tasks like grocery shopping, carrying large items, or transporting children can be tough on even the best of them. That’s what makes cargo bikes great—they can carry everything (and more!) that you can imagine.

As their name suggests, cargo bikes are designed to carry heavy, large, or awkward loads. Their extra hauling capacity makes cargo bikes incredibly useful for families, commuters, and riders in cities, suburbs, and small towns across the country. Bicycle brands produce cargo bikes in several distinct layouts to meet the needs of riders seeking to carry or move more stuff by pedal power.

Almost any bicycle purpose-built to carry passengers or extra gear—such as packages, bags, or boxes—can be called a “cargo bike.” Cargo bikes typically feature reinforced frames, racks or mounting points, and come with higher payload capacities than traditional commuter, city, or townie bikes. Bike brands and third-party manufacturers also offer a wide array of accessories to outfit a cargo bike for your specific needs and use cases.

Bicycling’s editors are huge fans of cargo bikes, and we use them regularly for our daily commutes, running errands, dropping kids at school, and family rides. Like other bicycle types, cargo bikes come in all shapes and sizes—and there’s almost certainly one that’s perfect for you. Finally, while non-assisted cargo bikes are available, electric-assist cargo bikes are now far more common. So all of the models we test use electric motors.

According to recent reports, buying Tip: Consider where you will store your cargo bike. Their large size and extra weight can make cargo bikes difficult to store if you don’t have a garage or dedicated bike storage. If you need to park your cargo bike outside, get a heavy-duty bike lock and a bicycle cover to keep it safe.

Some cargo bikes are loaded with features but cost too much, while others are low-priced but don’t ride well. However, the Aventon Abound LR is the rare $2,000 electric cargo bike that doesn’t feel like a compromise—And that’s why it’s our Best Overall pick.

It has been revealed that the Abound LR is built to handle daily life—daycare drop-offs and pickups, grocery runs, and commuting—without the premium price tag of its competitors. Plus, it rides with more polish than some bikes costing twice as much. This makes it a great option for families and utility‑minded riders. The LR can handle kids, panniers, and weekly shopping trips without stretching the budget. It’s ideal for those who value comfort and stability over top‑end speed.

Sources indicate that if you’re comparing this Aventon to other electric cargo bikes, it feels more polished than budget longtails like the Lectric Xpedition 2.0 and Rad Power’s Rad Wagon 5. Yet, the Abound LR costs far less than premium mid‑drive cargo rigs from Tern, Cannondale, and Trek.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it’s one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around. The dual-battery model ($1,799) boasts an incredible 120-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. This makes the XPedition an option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

In a recent development, “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, remarked Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

However, concessions had to be made somewhere to reach this low price, and the result is a somewhat cheap feel. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but it is erratic at times. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend.

Sources indicate that tern’s Quick Haul Long is enticing because it delivers the core functionality of the pricier GSD series at a lower price. While the Quick Haul Long’s frame isn’t as sleek as the GSD and lacks a suspension fork, the bike still has everything needed to be a true car replacement.

The Quick Haul features include hydraulic disc brakes, a robust double kickstand, a built-in frame lock, trailer attachment points, and an impressive maximum weight limit of 419 pounds. Tern also offers a wide range of accessories to customize the bike to your individual needs. Even when loaded with two kids and a trailer full of groceries, the Bosch Cargo Line motor handles the load with ease. However, don’t expect a speedy ride when fully laden. The bike can handle the load (and you’ll get where you want to go), but it won’t zip to its maximum pedal-assist speed of 20 mph when weighed down.

If you like the look, features, and price of Aventon’s Abound LR but want a smaller package, the SR is the bike for you. The SR has the same 440-pound carrying capacity and 60-mile range as its longtail sibling, but on a shorter wheelbase chassis. This makes it ideal for riders with space constraints (such as apartments and RVs) or anyone seeking a quick ride around town.

The Specialized Globe Haul ST packs 419 pounds of cargo capacity into a surprisingly compact frame. With powerful brakes, dialed geometry, and well-thought-out features, it’s ready for commuting, grocery getting, neighborhood errands, or getting a child to daycare. Without active suspension, the Haul relies on massive 3.5-inch tires for its ride comfort, which work well on all but the roughest roads.

My partner, Julia, purchased a Haul ST after reading the Bike of the Year review. She uses it for commuting in Boston and describes the Haul as zippy. She mentioned, “The power levels are flexible, and I can easily adjust them to how I want to ride or tackle hills.” She also likes the cargo configurations for carrying groceries and running errands. Julia also likes the Haul’s geometry; “It’s nice to ride upright, and it gives me more visibility.”.

It has been revealed that the fresh third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that the Fetch+ 4 is Trek’s take on the classic Dutch bakfiets. This bike is essentially the minivan of bikes—it carries up to four kids. It includes two child seats, but you can add accessories to improve your passengers’ comfort. These include a full cover for the basket to keep everyone out of the wind and rain. To power the Fetch, Trek uses Bosch’s BES3 system with a Bosch Cargo Drive motor. It delivers power via a Gates Carbon belt drive for virtually maintenance-free operation.

It has been revealed that most families know Radio Flyer for its iconic red wagons, tricycles, and ride-on toys, but did you know the company also made a range of electric bikes? I use “made” here because, unfortunately, Flyer is backing away from e-bikes to concentrate on its core business. However, if you buy this bike, you’ll still have after-purchase support and the brand will have spare parts available.

It has been revealed that the Loop is a 20-inch-wheel mid-tail model equipped with a 750W hub motor (87Nm torque) and can carry up to two children as passengers. Like a good family bike, Flyer loads the Loop with safety features, including a fully enclosed rear wheel, long front fender, turn signals, and four-piston Magura hydraulic disc brakes. Flyer offers the Loop in one universal frame size (fitting riders 4’11” to 6’3”) and four color choices.

Health & Fitness Editor Monique LeBrun tested the Loop with her six-year-old daughter for several months. “I’ve never ridden an e-bike before, so I was a little skeptical about it, but I really enjoy riding the Radio Flyer,” she said. Lebrun notes that “the seat is very comfortable, and I love that it has a low frame so I can easily step on and off the bike.”.

The Tern GSD redefines what a car-replacement bike can be. It’s easy to picture running errands on a cargo bike if you live in a city or a town with great cycling infrastructure. However, many people live in suburbs or other areas not exactly designed for bike commuting. The GSD’s Class 3 Bosch pedal-assist motor, massive cargo capacity, and solid battery range make long hauls realistic, even for riders who live miles from town.

Riders from 5 feet to 6’6” can share the same bike, thanks to quick-release adjustments on the seatpost and handlebar. The bar can even rotate forward for tall riders who want extra reach. The bike also features premium touches you won’t find on low-cost cargo bikes—like a suspension fork, Magura 4-piston hydraulic brakes, an integrated lock, and a suspension seatpost. Practical design details make storage and transport surprisingly manageable: the handlebar folds at the headset, the seat drops quickly, and the whole bike can be tipped upright to rest on its rear rack—perfect for tight garage corners. However, be aware that the GSD’s extra weight can make loading it into a vehicle a two-person task.

Industry observers note that do you need to carry absolutely everything and want to do it in style? If so, an Urban Arrow might be right for you.

Sources indicate that this front-loader, basket-style cargo bike is designed for families and people carrying large items like multiple kids, large dogs (plural), a Costco run, or a couch—All things people can carry with an Urban Arrow. Thanks to its 75 Nm Bosch Cargo Line motor and 545Wh battery, it has the torque and range to carry you and your stuff up hills and to your destination without breaking a sweat.

According to recent reports, domestic and international cargo bike popularity has exploded in the past decade, notes Xtracycles founder and longtail cargo bike pioneer Ross Evans. There are generally four main styles of cargo bikes: longtail, short-tail, front loader, and the bakfiet (a Dutch term that translates to ‘box bike’). You can also find trike varieties for riders needing to transport heavy loads or more than two children.

➡️ Longtail cargo bikes are the most agile and lightweight design. They transport cargo or passengers on an extended tail section behind the rider.

➡️ Short-tail cargo bikes are a variant of longtail bikes, but with a shorter rear extension that makes them more compact and better suited for those tight on space.

➡️ Front loader bikes place the payload in front of the rider, generally on a low-slung platform adaptable to suit many needs.

➡️ Bakfiet-style bikes feature a large basket (typically in front of the rider) for carrying cargo or transporting multiple passengers.

Recent findings suggest that moving hundreds of pounds on a bike without a motor is great...if you want to get a workout. But most riders and families don’t want that stress or extra work. That’s why we recommend electric motor-equipped cargo bikes. “Electricity and cargo bikes go together like PB&J,” Evans claims. E-cargo bikes feature pedal-assist electric motors that can deliver more than 50 miles of range. This makes cargo bikes more accessible to riders who want car-like convenience in a bike-sized package.

However, the tech comes at a price: Electric cargo bikes are pricier than their non-electric counterparts. Unless you live somewhere completely flat, we think an e-cargo bike is the best choice. Electric motors vastly improve a cargo bike’s usability and can save you money in the long run by making it a more effective car substitute.

In a recent development, once you’ve purchased a cargo bike, you’ll want the right accessories to maximize its utility. Start on the manufacturer’s website: Many brands sell panniers, racks, and child seats to match their cargo bikes. Alternatively, if your style is more “dump it and go,” bakfiets use a single spacious box—typically upfront—that’ll fit all your stuff (there are still seat belts for your kids). The best way to determine which style or bike you prefer is to take bikes for test rides.

It has been revealed that approach an e-cargo bike and accessory purchase the same way you would if buying a car. Try and test as many options as possible. Prioritize your most common cargo needs. While it can be fun to think in aspirational terms, a bike suited to your daily needs means you use it more often.

These bikes are thoroughly put through their paces by the Bicycling test team. We don’t only test them—we live with them. We haul groceries, drop kids off at school, and squeeze in as many rides as possible to see if these e-cargo bikes can truly replace our cars for daily life. Test Editor Dan Chabanov puts them through the ultimate car-replacement experiment on the streets of his hometown of Philadelphia, and Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy tests them on her daily commute to the office. A.

t our Easton, Pennsylvania headquarters, the rest of the team gives these bikes a daily beating, using them to run errands around town (because let’s be honest—e-cargo bikes are just plain fun to ride). We also speak with the product managers behind the designs to understand their choices, and compare each model to its closest competitors to see how they stack up. Bottom line: we test these bikes like we’d use them in real life—because we actually did.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

  • When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“.

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.).

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

Recent findings suggest that the drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again rapidly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

In a recent development, A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

It has been revealed that “Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”.

This got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”.

That win got them back on the routine.

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

It has been revealed that “How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”.

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”.

It’s getting the next available win.

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

Industry observers note that to be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.).

“Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪.

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”.

According to recent reports, this is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence states that something SIGNIFICANT needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:.

This is one piece of how our coaches do accountability. Here are a few more ideas for you:.

#45319. Latest Update: I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1516 w)

Latest Update: I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body.
  • I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace.
  • “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images).

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”.

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

In a recent development, but I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

It has been revealed that I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”.

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

My doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I stated.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”.

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A significant reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my massive question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

It has been revealed that there’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, claims David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

“When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”.

According to recent reports, in another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he stated.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, says it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running indicates that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

“When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he states. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”.

In a recent development, instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor stated my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment quickly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

Recent findings suggest that but as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon prepares, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

It has been revealed that what I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

It has been revealed that he reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he noted gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”.

Sources indicate that his advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, indicates Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

Sources indicate that and, Moffat says, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

Industry observers note that “The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she notes. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”.

In fact, she says, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

In a recent development, as for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

It has been revealed that GLP-1 medications change how the body regulates appetite, weight, and energy. That means the nutrition, exercise, and recovery strategies professionals typically use may need to change, too.

For example, a client with a dramatically reduced appetite may struggle to get enough protein and essential nutrients. Someone who’s losing weight promptly may also be losing strength or struggling to recover from workouts that used to feel manageable.

Others may experience medication-related side effects, changes in their relationship with food, or plateaus that require a different approach.

Effective GLP-1 coaching means understanding these physiological changes and knowing how to adapt your support accordingly.

It also means recognizing when a client’s needs go beyond coaching and require input from their prescriber or another healthcare professional.

Bored With Your Workout? Try a Latest Level, Not a New Program

  • When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.
  • Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the client story this comes from.

This was the first thing a latest client mentioned to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.

-> See something new, give that a try.

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

In a recent development, she was moving. She was trying fresh things. She was having fun (at least at first).

But she was frustrated with herself.

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something upcoming is exciting.

It has been revealed that A upcoming program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

Industry observers note that and that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a substantial part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

According to recent reports, getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”.

It’s “how do I keep some of that newly introduced-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐.

That’s what we worked on together.

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:.

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”.

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

When she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: newly introduced reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

So something was always changing.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

But the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

She still fell off some. (Life happens.).

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

But that was a choice, not a restart.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a new program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight).

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with fresh reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

📅 23 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • Sources indicate that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

Sources indicate that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

While they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

The Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for new riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

The Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

Industry observers note that cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

Industry observers note that the CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

Sources indicate that based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

In a recent development, brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a substantial enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

If you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

Want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

In a recent development, priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the New York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

In a recent development, the Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

Industry observers note that test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

Industry observers note that “At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he mentioned. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

Want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

Most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Sources indicate that intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

Recent findings suggest that while the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

Sources indicate that this FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

According to recent reports, if you want big tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

Even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

Sources indicate that the Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience reveals in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

The Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Industry observers note that many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

It has been revealed that alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

The Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

Recent findings suggest that most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

Below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

It has been revealed that this relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

The Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

Many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

Since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

In a recent development, when shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

Lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Sources indicate that once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

In a recent development, complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

It has been revealed that picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards.

Avios One-Way Off-Peak Business.

US Gateway Cities with Nonstops.

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

It has been revealed that that's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

It has been revealed that marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

Sources indicate that one important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

Industry observers note that go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Sources indicate that before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Industry observers note that award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:.

It has been revealed that most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

In a recent development, it's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

Recent findings suggest that the cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

It has been revealed that now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

According to recent reports, do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike. Admittedly, I’ve been the ringleader on more than one occasion for a solidly underbiked ride that was listed as a gravel ride.

There are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel. Some pride themselves on challenging and chunky gravel roads, while other places have gravel rides with a 10,000-foot view. And how each rider defines gravel will be different from person to person.

The definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits. Many areas of the country may boast one great gravel quality, but this list compiles the places that check off more than a few boxes.

At this point, it’s clear gravel riding is here to stay, but the challenge lies in deciding where to ride first. Our list has the best gravel riding pockets in the country and can serve as your checklist for 2027. The last destination on the list is a sleeper you shouldn’t miss.

The Latest York Times featured a run-down of the best spots in the U.S. for gravel biking, so you know it’s now officially mainstream. Their list included Northwest Arkansas, namely Bentonville—in the heart of the Ozark Mountains—which has become known as a gravel (and all things biking) hub. That’s thanks in large part to the Walton family. The Waltons own Walmart and run the Walton Family Foundation, which has always prioritized bikes and outdoor recreation.

If you’re in the area, there are endless ways to spend a day on a bike. According to the NYT, Chuck Campbell, an environmental manager for a wastewater recycling firm, has designed several epic loops that together make up the 1,200-mile Arkansas High Country Route, a mix of paved and unpaved roads that launched in 2019.

Industry observers note that colorado might be home to the unique gravel races of any state, but if you’re looking for gravel events you can likely find one in just about any state these days. Steamboat Springs debuted SBT GRVL in 2019. They’ve since grown to be one of the most inclusive events out there, with all kinds of training ride opportunities, and partnerships with inclusive cycling groups such as All Bodies on Bikes and Ride for Racial Justice.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a quieter way to enjoy Colorado gravel, check out Nederland, a quaint mountain town 30 minutes outside of Boulder. There are probably more gravel roads in and around Nederland than paved, and almost all of them take you to excellent cafes and snack shops to recharge. Nederland to Gold Hill with a homemade slice of pie from the Gold Hill Store is tough to beat.

If you’re looking for a way to escape the cold in the coming months, Arizona offers tons of gravel-friendly riding. Many of the multiuse trails around the Phoenix State Parks can be connected for some hearty loops. AZ Gravel Rides has compiled an excellent list of gravel adventures in all areas of the state.

In a recent development, patagonia, Arizona, has become a not-so-secret winter escape for gravel lovers lately. Located in the Patagonia Mountains, it’s got a desert mountain feel, with plenty of climbing and lots of sandy roads with incredible views. The area is expansive, so you can ride all day without seeing anyone. According to the NYT, “a newly introduced edition in the expanding “Gravel Adventure Field Guide” series focuses on routes in Patagonia and surrounding Santa Cruz County.”.

Sources indicate that and on the East Coast, Vermont can’t be beat. Most people in Vermont will probably tell you that they prefer dirt roads to paved ones. There’s something nice about a slower pace. Seven Days VT claims that Vermont has 8,579 miles of unpaved roads, compared to 7,182 miles of paved roads.

Sources indicate that the VTXL is a 300-mile route that stretches from Canada to Massachusetts via 90 percent dirt and gravel roads. Former WorldTour rider turned adventure/gravel pro Ted King is at the moment bikepacking the route that he’s done before in a single push. This time he’s documenting the summer’s flooding that ravaged the state. “Heartbreaking but with short memories, we want to help bring attention to just how devastating it was and continues to be as Vermont rebuilds,” he posted to social media.

The gravel in Vermont is extensive, but make sure you tie in a climb up the road dubbed, “the steepest paved mile in the U.S..” Lincoln Gap may be known for having the steepest paved mile in the US, but the descent down from the climb is high quality gravel. Just a heads up—if you’re a fan of breweries, then plan for more stops than you would normally expect.

According to recent reports, when I think of a great area for riding gravel there are some factors that the location needs to have. Hard gravel climbs with ripping descents, some views while you catch your breath on top of the climbs, and something for everyone to ride—regardless of skill level, are a few things that top my list. Northern Pennsylvania may not be among the top areas for gravel riding for many people, but it should be.

It has been revealed that rail trails like the Pine Creek Rail Trail leave an option for anyone to get out on gravel in this area, but there are plenty of options for the seasoned cyclists as well. Events like Endless Mountains, Unpaved Pennsylvania, and Lu Lacka Wyco Hundo boast routes from 50 miles to 430 miles long. For context—the 115-mile route of Endless Mountains had over 12,000 feet of climbing. A large majority of the route was on gravel with very little stretches of paved country roads.

In a recent development, while the views from the top of the hills are beautiful its worth noting you don’t have the vistas of other locations like Colorado or Arizona. The area makes up for it’s lack of high alpine overlooks or desert landscapes with tough, punchy gravel climbs and positive vibes from the locals. Make sure this unexpected gravel honey hole ends up on your destination list for 2027. If you think I missed a spot (or have somewhere I should add for my 2027 ride list), then drop it in the comments below.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know.
  • Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules.
  • In a recent development, however, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family).

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

In a recent development, however, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:.

According to recent reports, 2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

Recent findings suggest that 3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

Sources indicate that 6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

Industry observers note that 7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

Recent findings suggest that 9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

It has been revealed that 13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

Recent findings suggest that 15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

Sources indicate that 16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”.

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

It has been revealed that 21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

It has been revealed that 22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

Sources indicate that 23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

Sources indicate that 24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

In a recent development, 25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

Industry observers note that 26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes.

According to recent reports, 27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, noted it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

According to recent reports, I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

In a recent development, you were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

It has been revealed that after multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s vital to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

According to recent reports, you know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Recent findings suggest that try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

It has been revealed that and if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

In a recent development, if you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.
