Breaking: 5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.
  • A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants.
  • This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts showed significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, indicates Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”.

In a recent development, julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she says, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Industry observers note that convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

According to recent reports, cyclists who are entirely fresh to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue says. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Industry observers note that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

It has been revealed that start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Recent findings suggest that start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Sources indicate that stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

This workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

According to recent reports, stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Recent findings suggest that holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Recent findings suggest that A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural complications, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Sources indicate that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

In a recent development, lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Sources indicate that start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

According to recent reports, stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

According to recent reports, start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue indicates.

Recent findings suggest that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

Industry observers note that stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

If you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

It has been revealed that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Recent findings suggest that stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

According to recent reports, lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

#45306. How Yoga Supported Me Through Cancer (In Ways That Had Nothing to Do With Movement)

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1400 w)

How Yoga Supported Me Through Cancer (In Ways That Had Nothing to Do With Movement)

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “You’ll need surgery,” my doctor said.
  • Recent findings suggest that moments before, she had informed me that I had endometrial cancer, and it felt as if an anvil had landed on my chest.
  • It has been revealed that yoga was the practice I turned to whenever life got substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Canva; Sean Musil | Unsplash).

In a recent development, “You’ll need surgery,” my doctor said. “After that, no yoga.”.

Recent findings suggest that moments before, she had informed me that I had endometrial cancer, and it felt as if an anvil had landed on my chest. My mind flooded with questions I couldn’t yet articulate. Somewhere in that static, I tried to recall exactly what she remarked about the diagnosis. And wait, no yoga?

It has been revealed that yoga was the practice I turned to whenever life got substantial. And this was huge. As my doctor explained the “good news” was that we caught the cancer early, and if all went well I wouldn’t need chemo, I tried to focus. She remarked I’d likely need a full hysterectomy, followed by months of recovery with limited movement. My heart sunk. How was I supposed to navigate cancer without the thing that always helped me navigate all the other things?

I immediately stepped into a new rhythm, my calendar filling with appointments for testing, bloodwork, and specialists. I wrote down hospital addresses and watched as needle after needle entered my veins. I freaked out as bills racked up and I had to repeatedly check in with my insurance manufacturer because things were insanely complicated. I tried to let go of control where I could and take charge where I needed. It was exhausting.

Recent findings suggest that at each appointment, I had to tell the cancer story all over again. As I traveled around Upcoming York City, I secretly hoped I’d find someone who would tell me this was all a mistake. It felt like my body had betrayed me or that I was suddenly in skin that wasn’t my own.

In a recent development, most of the time I left a doctor’s office and went straight to a yoga class. I needed to feel my feet underneath me, to soothe my mind and heart with deep breaths. I told myself I was going to practice yoga as much as I could in the months leading up to surgery, almost as if I could stockpile it in my bones. It was often the only time I felt at home in my body.

Sources indicate that yoga provided a hum of consistency. There, on the mat, I felt that familiar alchemy of turning my anxieties over to the practice. I breathed. I moved. During these months of consultations and biopsies and test results, yoga was the only time I felt okay, sometimes even good, in my body.

Yet sometimes in Down Dog, it felt like my entire heart turned into a teardrop, heavy with emotion. I cried in Child’s Pose, processing the layers of emotions associated not just with the cancer but the fact that I’d be losing a part of my body.

Other times, I was hit with denial, fear, and shock. How had this happened? I was only in my 40s, and the most common age range for endometrial cancer was the 60s. Sometimes, lying in Corpse Pose, I’d let myself think about the truth underlying cancer, feeling my mortality. I was staring impermanence in the face.

Recent findings suggest that yoga was a place to feel all the things. Yet more often than not, I ended practice feeling awash with a rare calm I no longer took for granted. I wished I could escape into the post-yoga glow forever. I was clinging! Still, I wished there was a way.

The day of my surgery finally came, and it was time to say goodbye to my cancer, my uterus, and, at least for a while, yoga.

Industry observers note that that morning, sitting in my hospital gown on a gurney waiting to enter the OR, I tried to stay centered, but my body took over. I broke out in a cold sweat. Nausea rolled through me and my breath caught in my chest. The room swirled.

“You’re having a panic attack,” my doctor said, placing her hand on my back. I inhaled and exhaled for a count of five, over and over, instinctively practicing box breathing while trying not to jostle the many tubes hooked to me. My body knew this language. It eventually began to calm down.

It has been revealed that in the days after surgery, my pelvis blared with pain. I couldn’t even sit up on my own in bed without wanting to pass out. Lying motionless and still feeling discomfort, I began to understand what the doctor had meant by taking a break from the poses. I couldn’t just unroll my mat and fall into Child’s Pose.

But I was starting to sense the ways yoga was still with me, even approaching me in this moment of pain and need.

Sources indicate that while stuck in bed, I thought of the yoga teaching of purusha and prakriti. Purusha is the witness self, the spirit, the part of us that watches our experiences. Prakriti is the material world, including the body. As I cared for myself, taking my medications on a complicated rotation and hobbling around throughout the day to avoid blood clots, I realized I could watch my body yet also dwell in a different part of myself. I felt a small space between my body self and my witness self, and this space felt like a lifesaver.

Propped up by pillows, I listened to a recording of a yoga nidra guided meditation. The voice brought my awareness to various parts of my body that I hadn’t contemplated in months. One of my teachers, Dharma Mittra, had described yoga nidra as closing the open tabs on your computer, or your thoughts, while keeping the computer, or your consciousness, on.

Now I closed down one thing at a time, mentally minimizing the cancer, the pain, even the act of healing, and felt into the parts of me beyond that. I breathed and observed.

According to recent reports, I felt inside me a quiet resilience I’d spent years getting to know and grow on the mat. I was in a forced state of slowing down, and here I saw a glimmer of an unprecedented intimacy with my life that no Netflix binge would blot out.

As I began to move through healing, I realized even pursuing treatment had been ahimsa, or non-violence practice, toward myself. I began to understand that my body hadn’t betrayed me. It was still my friend, just someone going through something, and my practice had been to try to be kind to it, advocate on my own behalf.

Coming to terms with cancer and the impermanence of my body had been a kind of satya, or honesty, practice. Walking the healing path and heading into surgery had been a sort of act of surrender, ishvara pranidana. Somewhere along the way I’d released into a kind of trust and faith that I would be carried by a higher power.

Sources indicate that I realized there was so much of the yoga practice already deeply within me beyond the poses. It was a relief: yoga wasn’t going anywhere. Neither was I. The practice’s philosophy and lessons were an invisible scaffolding supporting all aspects of my life. I even felt a sense of joy remembering I was more than my body.

Recent findings suggest that yoga was strengthening me just when I most needed it. It was teaching me about myself, a kind of svadhyaya, or self-study.

Sources indicate that yoga didn’t “save” me. It didn’t distract me from the realities of my situation. What it did was provide me with tools and a framework for navigating those realities and remaining acutely present with myself throughout the better part of a year. I had built these tools over decades of practice, and they were indeed inside me, deeper than I even knew.

I’d given myself to yoga years earlier. Now, it was giving back to me.

It has been revealed that A few months after my surgery, I went to yet another post-op appointment. I was tired of being poked and prodded, but as my doctor checked my stitches, I stepped into the role of witness again, more consciously this time.

“You’re cancer-free!” she said, reviewing the final pathology report. “You’re now a cancer survivor. You can go back to yoga now.”.

I didn’t tell her, but I’d been practicing all along.

#45304. Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)

Turn Your Pool Workout Into Playtime With These Game-Inspired Exercises

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable.
  • We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Turn your swim workouts into games with these fun ideas for making the pool more enjoyable. (Photo: Challenge Family).

We know all the excuses to skip a swim because we’ve used many of them ourselves. Either it’s too cold outside or it’s too beautiful a day to pass up a bike ride. Or perhaps there’s a storm 100 miles away that might suddenly decide to blow right over the aquatics center. But the truth is, if your workout is interesting enough, you’ll have all the excuses you need to get yourself into the pool, not out of it.

And we’re not just talking about adding in a random drill here and there. Gamifying your swim workout, whether through solo exercises or team activities, helps make a workout enticing enough that you’ll want to do it over and over again. Adding an element of play to your swim can make it more challenging, productive, and fun all at once.

Sources indicate that before we get into a handful of our favorite games and drills, we asked Sage Hopkins, head coach of Women’s Swimming & Diving at San José State University, for his tips on how to make swimming more enjoyable. With these tools in your arsenal, you might not skip your pool workouts anymore, but actually look forward to them instead.

Industry observers note that first, Hopkins stresses how crucial it is to hear laughter echoing across the pool deck. This might not be possible if you’re training alone, but if you have a training buddy who always keeps you smiling, make it a priority to meet with them more regularly. Hopkins also encourages using music to establish an upbeat atmosphere; that might look like playing a pump-up song on your way to the pool, or investing in a pair of swimming headphones to keep the tunes going lap after lap.

Recent findings suggest that once you know your purpose, Hopkins states, it’s easier to figure out what kinds of activities will make swimming more meaningful and enjoyable. Those who enjoy the camaraderie aspect of swimming and triathlon will enjoy team games like sharks and minnows.

Even simple details like naming a set, Hopkins claims, can add a thrill to swimming. If there’s a test set you’re always dreading, give it a quirky or amusing name to make it seem less intimidating. You could use the most challenging triathlon you’ve ever lined up for as inspiration (The Wales One Hundreds, for instance, or the Norseman No Breathers).

Now, without further ado, let the games begin!

Industry observers note that you don’t need any fancy clubs to play a round of swim golf — just enough glycogen in your head to add numbers. Hopkins suggests this drill for data-driven triathletes because it’s easy to keep track of your progression over time. Essentially, you add the number of strokes with the number of seconds that it takes you to complete a certain distance (such as 50 yards) to get a “score.” You’ll then repeat that distance several times within a single set, trying to keep your score as low as possible. This game helps improve your distance per stroke and ultimately conserve energy.

Industry observers note that healthy suspense invites bursts of dopamine and curiosity into your workout, and it also means that there’s no one to blame but fate for back-to-back sprint sets. Make sure to write the following rules down on a whiteboard or protected piece of paper to reduce confusion.

Sources indicate that start by grabbing a set of waterproof playing cards, and assign a technique to each suit; for example, spades might call for kicking, hearts for drills, diamonds for swimming, and clubs for pulling. Next, assign a distance to groups of numbers (for instance, 2s and 3s might mean 50s, while 4s and 5s might mean 100s, and so on). Keep your jacks, queens, kings, and aces in a separate pile because they’ll dictate the number of repeats (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively).

Recent findings suggest that so, for example, pulling a 5 of clubs alongside a queen would require you to grab your pull buoy for 2×100. Pulling a 2 of hearts alongside an ace would mean a 5×50 drill.

According to recent reports, another way to bring a measure of unpredictability to your workout is to roll a single die four times to determine your next set. The first roll determines your technique (5s could require kicking), the second your effort level (perhaps 4s always mean sprints), the third your distance (1s could mean 50s), and the fourth your number of reps (anywhere from 1 to 6).

If you were on a summer swim team as a kid, chances are high you played many games of sharks and minnows. The game starts out with one “shark” who tries to tag all the other “minnows” as they swim from one side of the pool to the other. Each swimmer who gets tagged turns into a shark for the next round. You can complicate this game by instituting an underwater safety zone.

If you have an area of the pool to yourself, form teams, set up goals on opposite walls with pull buoys, grab a ball, and play water polo. This is an excellent way to make vertical kicking, sprinting, and treading water more exciting. It also facilitates team bonding.

Recent findings suggest that head to the deep end for this game to work on endurance as you tread water and practice vertical kicking. If the lifeguards allow it, you can play water volleyball over the flags with an inflatable beach ball. Your pool might even have a water volleyball net, and some versions float so that you can move them as required.

Hopkins recommends “call it sets,” inspired by Bob Steele, to work on pacing and fine-tuning your internal clock. Essentially, you and your training partners will swim a set of 100s, and before each repeat, each one of you will predict the time you expect to hit. Whoever is closest to their estimates wins the set.

Chase sets are a fun way for training groups with seemingly disparate ability levels to unite, says Hopkins. Slower swimmers are allowed a head start, while faster swimmers are tasked with trying to catch them. Chase sets are ideally employed for speedwork, not drills.

Recent findings suggest that casino night is extraordinarily fun for large teams and helps highlight everyone’s unique talents. First, two or three swimmers who are roughly equivalent in speed line up at the blocks. Then, the other teammates line up behind the swimmer they predict will win.

From there, you’ll use cards or dice to determine the “event” that the swimmers will be competing in (see general rules above in the solo workouts). Whoever has picked the winning swimmer gets a rest break while the rest of the team completes a penalty swim (a 50 sprint, perhaps). If you have one seemingly unbeatable swimmer on the team, you can assign them a permanent handicap.

#45303. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2327 w)

Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s.
  • Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong.
  • Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no significant deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he claims.

Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” indicates bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine.

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

According to recent reports, your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

According to recent reports, “Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” notes Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”.

According to recent reports, you may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

Sources indicate that A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

In a recent development, pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

According to recent reports, “When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”.

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie states. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research shows that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Recent findings suggest that of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, indicates Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very important when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier states. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”.

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:.

In a recent development, press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Industry observers note that hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

In a recent development, bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

According to recent reports, cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

It has been revealed that if you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

According to recent reports, finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent says. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent indicates.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, indicates Broadbent.

Having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt claims. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

An anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “massive three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

It has been revealed that how to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that mcGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Recent findings suggest that side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section).

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

Finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie states. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a big difference in your back health.”.

#45302. Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled.
  • First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory.
  • According to recent reports, rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which currently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

According to recent reports, rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which currently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

In a recent development, that means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Sources indicate that yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

Industry observers note that if he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and big swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

It has been revealed that if Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

Industry observers note that that’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

In a recent development, seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

Sources indicate that I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to initiative, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

It has been revealed that then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

In a recent development, stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

According to recent reports, after taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

According to recent reports, and what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

It has been revealed that with about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

But as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

10-Minute Morning Yoga Routine to Wake Up Your Entire Body

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need.
  • According to recent reports, so if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body.
  • No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this quick yoga flow at home is, as the name promises, a continuously moving, flowy vinyasa practice for full-body flexibility that moves your body in all the ways you need. Rather than holding poses for an extended period of time, you’re moving with your breath in a fluid and rhythmic 10-minute yoga routine that will definitely energize you and target your back, hips, and hamstrings.

According to recent reports, so if you woke up feeling a little sore or stiff, taking yourself through these movements can bring relief and get you feeling more comfortable in your body. I encourage you to choose a one-word intention for your day that you pause and focus on at the outset and throughout your practice. What is one word that captures how you want to feel today, what you want to focus on, or what matters to you right now?

No props are required although you are always welcome to use them anytime you would like more support.

Sources indicate that you’re going to start by targeting the spine. From your hands and knees, your palms go underneath your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. As you inhale, lower your belly, lift your gaze and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Recent findings suggest that as you exhale, reverse that motion. Thinking of pushing into your fingertips and knuckles, pushing the mat away from you, and letting your head release and your neck relax in Cat Pose.

And then go in between these two poses, getting into all parts of the spine, including the neck, upper back, mid back, lower back, all the way to your tailbone, trying to get that full range of motion.

Come back to hands and knees with a neutral spine.

In a recent development, still on your hands and knees, lift your right leg and trace some circles with it, as massive as you can, and then let’s reverse the direction of those circles. You’re simply trying to create movement through your right hip. You don’t need to overthink this one.

Step your right foot straight out to the side and press the outer edge of your foot against the floor. Lift yourself upright and reach your left arm overhead and toward the right in a side body stretch known as Gate Pose.

Sources indicate that come back to your hands and knees, tuck your toes, and hover your knees a little above the mat. You can probably feel your core engage.

It has been revealed that walk your feet back to keep your shoulders over your wrists in Plank Pose. Strongly press the mat away from you, drawing your lower belly inward and broadening through your upper back. Think of lengthening your tailbone toward your heels and drawing your lower belly inward and upward.

It has been revealed that let’s find Downward-Facing Dog. Lift your hips up and back, and peddle out your feet by straightening one leg and bending the other to stretch your ankles and calves. Keep your arms straight without locking your elbows. Feel the length through your spine.

Lower your knees to the mat and repeat the poses on your left side, including Hip Circles, Gate Pose, Hovering Tabletop, Plank, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward-Facing Dog, reach your right leg toward the sky, bend your right knee, open your hip, and take one more of those big hip circles from your Three-Legged Dog.

Industry observers note that from Down Dog, inhale as you step your right foot forward, spin your back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat as if you were coming into Warrior 2. Exhale as you flow into Extended Side Angle, bringing your right forearm onto your right thigh and reaching your left arm overhead.

As you inhale, straighten your front leg and reach your right arm all the way back in Reverse Triangle.

Then exhale back into Extended Side Angle, sinking your hips a little lower. Repeat that flow twice more like this.

Bring both palms to the mat on either side of your right foot and find Pigeon Pose from here. So take your right knee behind your right wrist and reach your left leg straight back. Inhale as you come high onto your fingertips to lift and lengthen, then exhale as you bend forward.

Move in between the two shapes twice more as you undulate through the spine. Then the next time you lower yourself close to the mat, stay here for 5 long, slow breaths. Try to release tension through your shoulder blades and arms.

When you’re ready, lift yourself off the mat and find your Downward-Facing Dog. If you like, you can first come forward into Plank and then lower yourself to the mat and take Cobra. Then repeat these poses on your left side, starting with Three-Legged Dog, Dynamic Extended Side Angle, and Dynamic Pigeon.

Come back to Downward-Facing Dog. Pause here for several breaths.

According to recent reports, bring your knees to the mat and take a seat. As with most morning practices, I don’t include a Savasana in case you might be tempted to fall back asleep, but you’re always welcome to take it on your own.

Industry observers note that sit tall and roll your shoulders down and away from your ears. Maybe you bring your hands together at the front of your heart. Pause here for as long as you can.

Thank you so much for doing this quick vinyasa flow at home with me. May you feel really good and have gotten a boost of energy. Let me know what your intention is for the day ahead in a comment below.

Promo Rewards Release Frequency.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Industry observers note that flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

Recent findings suggest that the transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

In a recent development, the practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that one nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

It has been revealed that finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

According to recent reports, unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Industry observers note that do this: Set a recurring monthly calendar reminder for Promo Rewards. Promo Rewards drop in the first week of each month and popular routes sell out fast. The readers who consistently land these redemptions aren't lucky — they're systematic. Mark the first Monday of every month as your "check Flying Blue" day.

Do this: Use an open-jaw routing to maximize your Europe trip. Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into one city and out of another within a single award booking. Fly JFK → CDG, travel through France, and fly home from AMS → JFK. You've just built a multi-city trip without paying for positioning flights — and used a single 53,000-mile award to do it.

Do this: Transfer points only after confirming availability. This cannot be overstated. Transfers from Chase and Amex are instant, but they are also irreversible. Never initiate a transfer until you have confirmed, with your own eyes, that the award seat is available and bookable. The five-minute shortcut of transferring first has stranded miles in countless accounts.

Sources indicate that avoid this: Booking standard dynamic awards without checking Promo Rewards first. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing on standard awards can be significantly higher than Promo Reward pricing — sometimes 30–50% more miles for the exact same seat. Always check if the month's Promo Rewards include your route before defaulting to a standard award.

Avoid this: Ignoring the surcharge line item. On standard (non-Promo) Flying Blue awards for Air France flights, carrier surcharges can add $200–$500 to your out-of-pocket cost. This doesn't eliminate the value, but it changes the math. Always review the full fee breakdown before confirming. Promo Rewards typically waive these surcharges — another reason to prioritize them.

Sources indicate that do this: Stack earning across multiple cards. You don't need to earn 53,000 points on a single card. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to Flying Blue at 1:1. Accumulate across programs, then choose the best transfer source when a Promo Reward surfaces. This flexibility is a structural advantage of the ChooseFI approach to travel rewards.

Industry observers note that know your expiry window. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one transaction (even a small earning or redemption) every two years to protect your balance.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Industry observers note that minimum requirements: You'll want at least 53,000 points in a single transferable currency (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt) or the ability to combine balances to reach that threshold. No Flying Blue status is required — this is available to any member.

Recent findings suggest that major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

Flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

It has been revealed that both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. Air France's cabin tends to emphasize French culinary presentation and wine service, while KLM has a more understated Dutch design aesthetic. Both are solid products. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Industry observers note that flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides
