8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix.
  • When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix.

Raw Nutrition Bum Hydration Fruit Punch.

Thorne Daily Electrolytes Blood Orange.

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

According to recent reports, but the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

It has been revealed that to be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health challenges (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”.

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition proposal. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

It has been revealed that with no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you initiative to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

It has been revealed that if you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is presently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.).

Industry observers note that with 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

According to recent reports, despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Recent findings suggest that led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

In a recent development, made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”.

Industry observers note that the flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

#45288. The Best Advanced GPS Running Watches of 2026, Tested by an Ultrarunner

📅 21 May 2018 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2699 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Advanced GPS Running Watches of 2026, Tested by an Ultrarunner

📅 21 May 2018 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • It has been revealed that I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up.
  • Sources indicate that as an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that I review a ton of running watches, cycling through all of the various features and idiosyncrasies to find which watch would suit which runner best, which watches deserve a place on our lists, and which don’t measure up. Sometimes, there are watches that are really cool, and do a lot of work, but they offer more than what the average runner needs to log their daily miles and monitor their fitness. But for backwoods adventure runners, ultrarunners, or runners who put a lot of demand on their machines, advanced GPS running watches like the ones on this list offer a bit more of everything—from cellular and satellite connectivity to off-road trail mapping to sturdier cases, more multisport functionality, and all around just more.

Sources indicate that as an ultrarunner, I am frequently testing watches for 50, 75, or even 100 miles at a stretch. Often these miles are spent deep in the woods in Upstate Upcoming York on trails that are poorly marked and pretty treacherous. Sometimes, there simply isn’t cell service to be had—anywhere. On top of that, I routinely test them during Hyrox, kayaking, paddle boarding, weight training, hiking, and even skiing—when there’s actually snow on the ground. My daily runs tend toward miles spent in New York City, which you wouldn’t think is an issue, but the tall buildings can thwart GPS pretty hard.

Looking for more running tech? Read our reviews of the best wireless headphones for running, headlamps for runners, and basic running watches.

Sources indicate that the Fenix 9 is not flawless, but dang, it is as close to it as I’ve ever tested.I’ve put over 300 miles on the Pro Solar, so I’ll get my little nitpicks out of the way first. Annoyingly, there’s a lag of about half a second to a second when you start a workout, and again when you switch between laps that the 8 did not have. It’s not the most annoying thing in the world, but alas. Also, the app is still the Garmin Connect app. (I will beat this drum until they fix it.).

It has been revealed that now? My happy place, the good stuff. The solar ring on the Pro Solar model puts this watch so far ahead of every other run watch on the market that it can’t even see the others from the rearview. The 51mm is rated for up to 57 days in smartwatch mode with solar, and the 47mm gets up to 34. In the 51mm’s max battery GPS mode, that stretches to 186 hours, or up to 1,000 with solar. I took this out in the backwoodsiest of backwoods Adirondack trails, where I forced it to rely wholly on satellite, and I ran it for 12 solid hours, and it barely ticked the battery.

In a recent development, and that multiband GPS with SatIQ? It’s the best in class, and it locks you down in a hurry. The inReach satellite connectivity lets me run those backwoods and feel safe about doing so. (Though, I still bring a SatCom.).

It’s built like a beast without feeling like one. This is the first Fenix with a titanium case, plus a sapphire lens and a 10 ATM water rating, so rain, sweat, and my early morning postrun ocean swims don’t screw it up.

It’s chockablock with performance and training metrics, and with Epic, their new multiday activity tracker, it’s better than ever. It’s light on the wrist, and it’s easy to use even with sweaty or sea salty fingers.

Industry observers note that my favorite little bonus is the flashlight. It’s dimmable and comes in white, red, or green, so it’s great for visibility on early morning runs and also for finding crap at the bottom of my purse.

The base Fenix 9 is a solid watch too, but the Pro Solar is the one I’d get. It’s simply a very fine watch.

You might not be familiar with this brand, but when I tell you, they are punching so far above their weight class with this watch that you would think a 10-year-old just knocked out Floyd Mayweather, I’m not kidding.

Sources indicate that the Amazfit Balance Ultra costs $599.99. For that you get a Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire lens, and a 10 ATM rating that also covers freediving and recreational scuba. It weighs 57 grams without the strap, which is a lot of watch for so little weight. It’s a bit on the thicker side, but not so high profile it’s going to get caught on doors.

Sources indicate that battery is where things start to get unbelievable. The 780 mAh cell battery is rated for up to 30 days of typical use and 10 with the always-on display. In accurate GPS mode you get 50 hours, and power-saving GPS stretches to about 90 in our testing. Unless you’re running through the weekend, you’ll hit your limit before the watch does.

Industry observers note that for tracking, it uses dual-band GPS across six satellite systems that ends up acting just like a typical multiband GPS on par with a Coros or a Suunto. That is clutch when you run between tall buildings or under tree cover and your watch would otherwise decide you swam across the Hudson. The 1.5-inch AMOLED screen is bright enough that it can be read in direct sun for the most part.

I will say that the dang buttons on the side are far too easy to depress, leading to accidentally starting activities, but overall, it’s incredible.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is a light upgrade from the 3. It has increased storage, an upgraded band, and introduces some more in-built activities like rucking and rowing alongside Garmin’s multiday training tool Epic. The Enduro line is built for multi-day trekking. Everything about it is engineered for endurance—the rugged design, precise tracking, and especially the solar-powered battery that seems to last forever. You don’t even think about charging most days; it just handles your training, races, and long trail days without missing a beat. The safety and satellite coverage give you extra peace of mind when you’re out alone, far from cell service or the nearest trailhead.

Two features stand out on every serious run. The Pack Weight tool adjusts your effort estimates based on how heavy your gear is, which makes your performance data feel more real—especially on long mountain efforts. And the Next Fork guide keeps you on track, showing how far it is to the next junction so that you don’t have to stop and fumble through maps. Add Garmin’s multiband GPS with SatiQ tech that automatically switches between the best systems into the mix, and logs routes that are spot-on, no matter how deep into the woods you go.

For ultrarunners or anyone training major, the Enduro 4 is reliability wrapped around your wrist—with battery life that feels almost unfair.

Industry observers note that I’ve been using the Suunto Vertical 2 off and on for a while now, and I’ve come to see it as a true multisport powerhouse rather than an everyday watch. It’s the one I pull out when training or adventures get serious—long runs, big mountain weekends, or backcountry routes where accuracy and endurance matter more than aesthetics. What sets it apart immediately are its maps—they’re crisp, easy to read, and fully offline, which makes navigation seamless even in the most remote terrain.

Battery life is another standout feature. The Vertical 2 easily lasts up to 60 days in smartwatch mode and delivers exceptional runtime with dual-band GNSS tracking, something that still amazes me every time I scroll through my recorded routes after multihour training blocks. The titanium and sapphire glass construction give it a premium, expedition-ready feel, and the watch itself feels built to handle harsh conditions without flinching.

Recent findings suggest that it’s definitely not what I’d wear every day—it’s large, rugged, and purpose-built—but that’s exactly the point. For athletes who bounce between cycling, running, skiing, hiking, and more, the Vertical 2 is a multisport dream, offering a level of mapping, tracking, and battery endurance suited for endless exploration.

The Garmin Forerunner 970 has been my daily watch for months, and it feels like the perfect blend of lifestyle usability and serious athletic performance. It’s light, comfortable, and sleek enough to wear all day—but underneath that understated design is a fully loaded training tool built for racing, coaching, and multidiscipline endurance work. Whether I’m tracking an interval session, planning an ultra-block, or guiding athletes through structured workouts, the 970 handles it all seamlessly.

It has been revealed that GPS precision is exceptional thanks to its multiband GNSS system, locking on rapidly and maintaining accuracy even through tree cover and narrow streets. The built-in coaching and training readiness tools have become part of my daily routine—providing recovery insights, suggested sessions, and race forecasts that actually feel tailored. For multisport training, it transitions modes smoothly, syncing effortlessly with sensors and Garmin Connect data.

As someone who loves to spend their hard-earned money on running in a pack of fellow weirdos at races, the pace predictor and race features are a big draw for the Garmin Forerunner 970. I sync my races from Garmin Connect, and the watch spits out predicted times for 5K up to marathons based on my VO2 max, training load, and recent runs, updating as I log more miles. What seals it for me are the race markers overlaid on the course profile, showing projected splits and elevation-adjusted pacing so I can visualize where to surge or conserve energy without second-guessing midrace. It's like having a personal coach whispering realistic goal times right before the gun goes off, turning pricey pack running into a heart-thumping hunt for a PR.

Battery life remains solid, though not as extreme as Garmin’s solar or expedition-focused models, lasting up to 20 days in smartwatch mode. Add in smart notifications, music storage, contactless payments, and wrist-based navigation, and it becomes a rare hybrid—a true performance watch that fits effortlessly into everyday life.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a vast improvement over the Ultra 3, which is a polite way of saying the Ultra 3 had room to grow.

According to recent reports, GPS now locks on fast. Apple states there’s no change here, but other members of my team and I noticed a difference. It might be in the software updates, but it’s better. I'm no longer starting runs before the watch has made up its mind. Once it has locked on, though, it commits to a story that isn’t quite true. Distance runs consistently one to one and a half percent long. During a marathon, that’s a few tenths of a mile I didn't earn.

Industry observers note that battery, thankfully, is finally impressing me. It’s leaps and bounds better, and it charges absurdly fast. I top it up while the coffee brews and I take my shower, and by the time I’m done, it’s fully loaded and ready to go.

Heart rate is the big jump. Against a Holter monitor, it stayed within two to three bpm on steady efforts. Run hard and it drifts to five to seven. I do wish it sampled my heart rate every second of every day instead of every five, but overall I don’t think the difference is huge, and when you combine that with the beauty of their apps, it’s hardly a thing.

According to recent reports, what’s missing for me is lactate threshold. I can live without many advanced run metrics, but I like knowing my threshold for training runs.

It has been revealed that in their fresh and improved health app, the ECG and hypertension alerts are useful, the cycle insights are spot on, and the morning report doesn’t make me feel graded. Transit pay, apps, and phone integration are unmatched. Satellite calling is extremely easy compared to any other watch I’ve tried. It’s a freaking great watch, overall.

When you step into the world of high-end GPS running watches, the sheer number of options can feel overwhelming—until you see the immense power packed into these bad boys. The essentials are non-negotiable: rock-solid multiband GPS precision, exceptional battery life (no one wants to lose tracking on a 50K run), accurate heart rate and recovery metrics, and seamless integration with your training looks. Every watch on this list delivers on those core requirements.

Where they start to spread their wings is everything layered on top. The bells and whistles are kinda wild. Things like dual-frequency GPS for navigating deep woods (or mountaintops), topo and trail maps that actually make sense when you’re lost, and multisport modes that keep up whether you’re running, swimming, skiing, triathlon training, or rolling through a Hyrox circuit. Barometric altitude readings, pulse ox sensors, and training readiness scores just round out the “how cooked am I?” data we’ve all come to both love and loathe in equal measure.

Industry observers note that some watches, though, don’t just tell you about your fitness—they could save your butt in a sticky situation. The Garmin Fenix 8 Pro works with Garmin’s inReach satellite system, letting you text or send an SOS nowhere near cell service. The Apple Watch Ultra takes a slightly different route with built-in satellite SOS and cellular, so if you’re off-grid and something goes sideways, you’re not shouting into the void. These are the kinds of features that make the difference between just tracking a run and actually trusting your gear if things go sideways.

Let’s be honest—most runners don’t need a watch this powerful. But if you’re out there chasing hours instead of miles, exploring trail networks that don’t even show up on Google Maps, or toggling between swim intervals, mountain climbs, and winter ski sessions, these make a world of difference. Basically, if you’re a runner like me with electricity in your veins and the ADHD that drives you toward multisport or off-the-beaten-trail running, these watches are for you.

Recent findings suggest that one of the quietest but most crucial reasons these watches shine is safety. With incident detection, live tracking, fall alerts, and SOS tools that actually connect you to help, they turn your wrist into a mini rescue hub. The Garmins can ping your emergency contacts automatically or connect through inReach. The Apple Watch Ultra fires off emergency signals via satellite if you end up out of range. And even the Suunto Vertical and Coros Vertix 2S earn their stripes here with detailed offline maps and batteries that cruise through multi-day efforts.

Basically, these aren’t just training tools—they’re peace of mind on your wrist. When you’re 10 miles deep in a trail system and the forest gets quiet, it’s nice knowing your watch is smarter about directions and safety than your phone or maybe even you.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and right now studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Sources indicate that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about tips for teaching yoga first appeared in the July-August 1997 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Recent findings suggest that I approached my earliest years of teaching with an enthusiasm that I hope helped make up for my lack of experience. As I look back now, in my 26th year of teaching, I realize that I have evolved a philosophy that shapes every class I offer. New teachers are usually so busy learning the craft of teaching that articulating a teaching philosophy remains a distant goal. Over time, though, we can evolve a style of teaching that expresses our values.

The following points express what I feel are imperatives for yoga teachers to remember while teaching.

As teachers, what we share with students can have effects that last far beyond the boundaries of class.

Sources indicate that the most key condition for a good yoga class is that it become a “sacred circle,” a term coined by author and Jungian psychologist Jean Shinoda Bolen. Each class must be a safe place for the personal exploration of body, emotions, and mind. A good teacher creates this sacred circle in which every student feels valued, respected, and completely safe.

The class must be free from verbal, emotional, physical, and sexual coercion or abuse. Without this intrinsic sense of safety, it is impossible for students to let go and allow the practice to unfold. In this context, safety means that the students retain the right to say no to working with a partner or to being adjusted or touched, and to say yes to moving at their own personal pace.

Look at each person individually and teach to that person in that moment. Each student is an individual to be guided, not a posture to be fixed. Often we focus too much on communicating about a pose instead of with a person. Your students might not remember the details of the asana (pose), but they will remember being seen, heard, and helped.

Humor teaches perspective and indicates your own humanness to students who might otherwise tend to put you on a pedestal. It also enables you to reveal yourself, thus encouraging your students to reveal themselves as well. Laughter improves our breathing by loosening the diaphragm, and helps us to remember that while yoga practice is important, it does not always need to be serious.

I don’t like the word “correct” when applied to teaching an asana since it implies that there is something wrong with the students—that they are less worthy for not “getting it right.”.

“Correcting” and “fixing” a pose sends the unconscious and therefore very powerful message that “it is never enough.” Many of us are already slaves to this judgment. Our houses are never clean enough, our meals never organic enough, our teaching never sophisticated enough. By constantly correcting students, you tell them that, once again, they are not doing enough.

According to recent reports, use your words, images, and very light and occasional touch, if welcomed, to transmit positive information. We need to make sure that students don’t harm themselves, but we also need to communicate that while there is always room to grow, where we are right now has a wholeness and beauty to it.

Sources indicate that are we teaching students to become like piano tuners who never experience the joy of just playing the piano? Do they know volumes about the technique, but nothing about the joy of practicing it? Without proper technique, the benefits of the pose will be lessened and injury can occur. But if technique is all we teach, then there is no heart in our teaching.

In the Yoga Sutras (11:1), Patanjali describes the dual concepts of abhyasa and vairagyam. Abhyasa, or “determined effort,” involves discipline, attention, and action, and it manifests as attention to the form of the posture. Vairagyam, on the other hand, is “supreme detachment.” Vairagyam is surrender, letting go, and allowing; it involves opening to the experience of the practice. When technique and form are balanced with heartfelt, free movement, then the asana is whole.

Recent findings suggest that learn how to teach the same poses in upcoming ways. The basic poses, repeated in almost every class, form the bedrock of teaching. If you are bored with them, change your practice so you can find something new in each pose each time. Also, remember that while you might be bored, your students probably are not.

Industry observers note that we all need repetition; it is really the only way we learn anything. If you have taught for some time, no doubt you have had more than one student come to you in amazement to report a “great insight” about a pose he or she just learned from another teacher. You might have been teaching this concept for years, but suddenly the student was ready to hear it.

It has been revealed that even as you repeat familiar poses, include something newly introduced in each class. It need not be a difficult posture or technique. It can be as simple as a new way to practice Savasana, but it will nonetheless keep your classes fresh.

“Listen” means observing with all your senses, as well as with your heart. Then teach from your heart what the students need right now. Do not be limited by what you think you “should” teach.

In a recent development, no matter how much training you have or how many years you have been teaching, each class is a newly introduced experience. Trust your intuition about what is appropriate in this moment and teach that.

For a couple of weeks after the San Francisco earthquake in 1989, my students found it almost impossible to practice standing poses. No one trusted the earth. Each time I would try to teach standing poses, students would have balance problems and become agitated. We all needed the reassurance of sitting down for a while. I responded to this obvious problem by focusing on seated poses, gradually reintroducing standing poses as it seemed appropriate.

Industry observers note that the body is programmed to move according to complex neurological and muscular patterns involving whole groups of muscles. We spend a great deal of teaching time trying to use words to isolate specific movements, when actually that is not how the body learns and remembers.

According to recent reports, when children learn a movement, they practice and experiment until they learn the muscle pattern which accomplishes that movement. Imagine trying to tell someone how to walk—explaining exactly which muscles to use as agonists, which as antagonists, and which as stabilizers. Walking is too complex an activity for someone to talk you through it.

Nevertheless, teachers are stuck with using words until the student understands a movement from within. So choose your words carefully. “Invite,” “entice,” and “allow” have a very different feeling than “push,” “tighten,” “stamp,” “grind,” and “cut.” In a recent class I suggested that students “conjure” the pose out of their bodies. Images such as these help the student bypass the linear left brain and access the right brain, where whole movements are understood.

Industry observers note that try focusing on one thing in each asana rather than loading the student down with information. In the information age, we are overburdened with facts. We can know everything about the pose and still be unhappy in our lives. While knowledge about the pose can be useful and even necessary, it will not provide us with what we all crave: peace of mind, clarity, and compassion.

Allow the experience of the pose to be the true teacher—not your words.

Sources indicate that let the last part of the class be simpler and the sequence will be more satisfying. Sometimes it helps to have a theme—a part of the body, for example—to focus on in every pose. Whatever you choose, allow the instructions to become simpler as the students slow down and internalize their awareness.

Sleep-deprived Americans desperately need rest. Give your students the gift of learning how to relax at will by lying down on the floor in relaxation pose. I never cease to be amazed to hear from students that Savasana was skipped in another class and labeled unimportant. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Sources indicate that studies document that relaxation lowers blood pressure and other physiological parameters associated with stress, including respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and brain waves. Relaxation measurably improves the function of the immune system.

Sources indicate that savasana teaches much more than relaxation. It teaches clearly and concretely the importance of being, not just doing. Our culture is very much a “doing” culture; we value action and results over being and awareness. Savasana might be the only time during the week that the student is quiet and present—not acting, not achieving, not sleeping. This is the beginning of meditation and an extremely key gift. Always allow 20 minutes for deep relaxation. [Editor’s Note: This article was written in 1997. We support a long Savasana! And it’s okay if you can’t allow 20 minutes for Savasana.].

The integrity of a teacher’s practice expresses itself in several ways. First and foremost, it reflects how the teacher lives his or her life. Honesty in living makes possible honesty in teaching. A teacher’s formal yoga practice should be regular, not haphazard. But most notable, this practice should include love for yourself and your students, as well as love of yoga and life itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme. The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour will kick off on Friday, July 30, and conclude on Saturday, August 7, after nine days of racing.

In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar. And looking at the 2027 route, we’re in for another nine days of aggressive racing, a hard-fought GC battle, and opportunities for a wide range of stage winners. Yet some route choices leave me lukewarm, and a few things are missing altogether. There’s no trek into the Alps or Pyrenees, no individual time trial, and still no Paris finale.

Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.

First, the highlights, starting with the three-day Grand Départ in England.

The 2027 route puts a lot of the fireworks up front, so there’s no easing into this Tour. It opens with a short, punchy 86km stage from Leeds to Manchester. Officially classified as flat, it still packs in three categorized climbs. So while the sprinters may get their chance at the first yellow jersey, it’s not guaranteed. Then comes a bumpy stage two that, a local tells me, is much harder on the legs than it looks on paper. And then we’ll get the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift’s first team time trial in London.

According to recent reports, leeds, Manchester, London. The 2027 edition will put women’s racing in front of millions. That’s a huge opportunity to draw roadside crowds and reach latest audiences. Those opening stages could also give the GC an intriguing shape. An early winner backed by a strong team performance in London might carry a rider in yellow deep into the race.

Then there’s the Puy de Dôme. The volcano occupies a special place in cycling history, having hosted 14 men’s Tour de France stage finishes, including the famous 1964 head-to-head between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor.

Recent findings suggest that A more recent memory of the Puy de Dôme is that of Matteo Jorgenson’s heartbreak on stage nine of the 2023 Tour. The American attacked alone with almost 50km remaining, only for Canadian Michael Woods to catch and pass him some 450 meters from victory. Jorgenson ultimately finished fourth.

It’s easy to imagine the volcano hosting another exciting chapter in the Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon//SRAM) and Demi Vollering (FDJ United–Suez) rivalry.

In 2025, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift delivered six different stage winners and three riders in yellow. This year, it was six and five respectively. The 2027 route should again give a broad cast of riders their chance, with plenty of terrain for versatile stage hunters alongside opportunities for the sprinters and climbers.

According to recent reports, that’s something I like about the Tour. A Tour stage can define a rider’s season; just look at the breakthrough victories of Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education–Oatly), and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance–Soudal) in years past.

The route opens the door to well-rounded riders, but the overall will still likely be decided on the final two mountainous days. But if climbing decides the Tour, I’d like to see some high-mountain racing in the Alps or Pyrenees. If the intention is to give more riders a shot at the GC, then I want to believe that they can actually take the yellow home, rather than just borrow it for a few days.

Of course, Vollering and Niewiadoma excel on punchy terrain too. And that’s part of my concern: different profiles don’t guarantee different outcomes. Perhaps the shorter climbs will keep more riders in contention, but I’m not convinced this route broadens the fight for yellow as much as it prolongs it.

It has been revealed that then there’s London. I’m excited about the setting, but the racing format leaves me underwhelmed. I prefer an individual time trial where every rider controls her own performance. No matter the timing rules, a team time trial tends to favor stronger, bigger teams, with more money to spend on a deeper roster, equipment, testing, and optimizing. A rider from a team with fewer resources could leave London with a time loss that reflects her team's budget more than her own performance.

Eighteen kilometers may limit the damage, but as 2024 highlighted, when Niewiadoma-Phinney won the overall by just four seconds, every single second counts.

While Britain gets the significant-city showcases, I feel roadside fans in France get a bad deal. The route bypasses the country’s largest cities on its way to a finale where spectator access remains uncertain.

It has been revealed that strict environmental protections are in place on Puy de Dôme, and organizers are still exploring if they can admit a limited crowd at the summit. I understand the need for protection, but a repeat of 2023’s empty upper slopes would be a lonely way to welcome in the Tour winner. If fans aren’t welcome, surely it’s worth asking whether this is the right place to finish.

Sources indicate that and while a summit finish can deliver exciting racing, I’m still waiting to see the women’s peloton finish on the cobblestones of Paris, same as the men. Wout van Aert’s victory in 2025 and Mathieu van der Poel’s all-out effort in 2026 were absolute highlights of those Tours for me. The Montmartre circuit has shown how much racing in Paris can offer, beyond a ceremonial procession. After watching Vollering and Niewiadoma duel in France and again in Montréal, with Marlen Reusser never far behind, I want to see what these women could do on those streets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that presently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

Sources indicate that the timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Recent findings suggest that deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

In a recent development, timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:.

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:.

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Recent findings suggest that sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare People Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

In a recent development, contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

In a recent development, timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:.

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Recent findings suggest that shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

In a recent development, no. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

In a recent development, technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

It has been revealed that some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

Industry observers note that in very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

In a recent development, A timeshare is a prepaid vacation strategy with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively newly introduced gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

In a recent development, when I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate issues and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

Industry observers note that after trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Industry observers note that adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Industry observers note that step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

Recent findings suggest that one easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

If they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore new wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

If you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

According to recent reports, A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

Sources indicate that on my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Tech Report: The Top 11 Women’s Running Shoes That Have the Comfiest Fit, Coziest Cushioning, and Most Responsive Ride

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 12, 2026: End-of-year sales have already taken off. Our Best Stability Shoe, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is now on sale with 19% off. (We are currently testing the newest model, the Adrenaline GTS 26.) Our Best for Speedwork Shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is also discounted with 20% off.

We are in a latest era of running shoes, from stacked super trainers to plated racers to gravel models decked out with bike-inspired treads.

The industry formerly criticized for “shrink it and pink it,” i.e., the practice of making smaller-size men’s shoes and slapping pink on them and calling them women’s shoes, has gone to great lengths crafting footwear that’s women-specific.

In a recent development, brands are taking care to produce shoes that accommodate the average woman’s foot shape: wider in the midfoot area, narrower around the heel. But don’t think this list is free of pink shoes. The traditionally feminine colors have been reclaimed by brands like Nike (turns out it’s flashy and easier to spot neon pink Alphaflys). Here you’ll find trainers of every color for all types of women’s feet and women runners.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Glycerin 23On a budget → Fresh Balance EllipseMostly a run/walker → Hoka Clifton 11On the path to recovery → Hoka Bondi 9Adding in speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLLogging long runs → Nike Vomero 18Racing a marathon → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3An overpronator → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25Suffering from bunions → Altra Torin 9Running on rail trails → lululemon WildfeelNew to technical terrain → Altra Experience Wild 3.

Recent findings suggest that runner’s World has been around for almost 60 years, providing news, fitness tips, and, of course, gear recommendations for runners. Our product guides for essentials like running shoes and shorts come from our hardworking test team, who put the latest and greatest running gear through their paces day in and day out. These selections come from Senior Reviews Editor Cat Bowen, who blazes the trails and is an ultramarathon beast, and me, Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer. I have written about running gear for a decade and hold an even longer Boston Marathon streak, beginning in 2013.

According to recent reports, we picked these shoes based on feedback from the runners who are part of our 300-runner-strong team of local wear-testers and the expertise of our editors. We evaluated every shoe over the course of at least 100 miles, paying attention to overall performance, comfort, ride, longevity, and value.

According to recent reports, to ensure our shoe recommendations are truly comprehensive and trustworthy, we grabbed a wide array of shoe types to put through our rigorous testing. This involved evaluating them across diverse terrains, including challenging trails, smooth tracks, varied road surfaces, and—of course—treadmills. Our massive wear-test team allows us to gather feedback from individuals ranging from sprinters to marathoners, runners of different weights and body types, those with different foot strikes, shoe needs, and biomechanics. By combining varied surface testing with a diverse runner pool, we learn a ton about each shoe’s performance and suitability for a wide range of people and individual experiences. Based on our extensive testing, the options below are presently the best running shoes for women.

In our testing, we found the Glycerin 23 excelled as a daily trainer over the Ghost 18 among women testers. The formerly max-cushioned Glycerin has evolved into an everyday shoe that you can take out on easy days to long runs. Our women testers preferred the Glycerin 23 over the Ghost 18 because of the shoes’ fit. Several testers reported hot spots in the Ghost 18’s bunion-prone area. The Glycerin 23, on the other hand, was praised for its broad platform, soft and plush knit upper, and ample wiggle room in the toebox.

“The shoe is cushioned in a way that makes me want to do all my long runs in them,” mentioned tester and Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “It doesn’t drag as some cushioned shoes do, but feels responsive. My go-to comparison of a cushioned shoe is the Saucony Echelon which I love for walking/hiking, but which I cannot do long miles in because the shoe drags, makes me work too hard. In comparison, the Glycerin is plushy but responds well to my moods and the corresponding pace changes.”.

Sources indicate that the shoe has Brooks’s DNA Tuned midsole foam, which was introduced in the even cushier Glycerin Max. The experience running on DNA Tuned is just like Černá described: plush, supportive, responsive, ideal for running long.

One of our women testers described the Ellipse v1 as “nearly perfect.”.

New Balance’s intent with the shoe was to provide a high-cushioned, trampoline-like bounce experience for recreation. It’s the kind of shoe you can wear for daily training, while you lace up in it for a casual, conversationally paced group run. The Ellipse was specifically made to make runs easier.

Recent findings suggest that fresh Foam X is dialed in to produce a foamy, high-rebound ride with reliable shock absorption. It’s a ride that makes me look forward to lacing up the Ellipse and taking it out for whatever kind of run my heart desires on the spot. The tweaked foam makes running in the soft, springy shoe feel like a treat.

Sources indicate that “The best word to describe the cushion is plush,” remarked tester Laura Parks. “It has the extreme cushion sensation of a Hoka Bondi without feeling the weight.” She described the ride as unlike any she’s had running in other Fresh Foam X models.

We’re still in the process of testing the Clifton 11, but the team is already loving the shoe weeks into testing. Everything we love about Hoka—plush cushioning, cozy fit, responsive midsole—is usually encapsulated in each iteration of the Clifton. The 11 is no exception. It was a hard follow after the ClifTEN, but the Clifton 11 makes runs feel effortless, thanks to the compression-molded EVA midsole foam, which provides high rebound and a comfy platform that pillows your foot.

Industry observers note that the shoe has Hoka’s Meta-Rocker geometry to promote smooth transitions. Sidewalls make the fit snug but not too narrow as the Hoka Bondi 9.

Recent findings suggest that the Clifton 11 is also excellent for run/walking because of that cushioned support and rocker geometry. These elements make the Clifton reliable at any pace.

In a recent development, the Bondi 9, one of Hoka’s plushest daily trainers, is somehow cushier and sleeker with this upgrade. Hoka added 10 mm to the midsole—but this shoe is no chonk. We even tested it sprinting on the treadmill; the supercritically foamed EVA provides high energy return and soft support. But we especially like using the shoe for run/walking and recovery.

Industry observers note that “The Bondi 9 delivers great protection with an amazingly smooth roll,” mentioned tester Tiffany Volpe. “I can see why there is so much hype behind the Hoka and [why it’s called] the Queen of Cushion. I felt like I was sitting down in the midsole. I felt locked in with ample protection especially in the tongue and collar.

“I found the Bondi a perfect recovery day shoe and one that I reach for when I just want to head out for a long slow run to clear my head.”.

The shoe was also rated high in stability among testers, and they appreciated the reflective, as well.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate boldly dubbed the Adizero Evo SL Shoe of the Year merely a month into 2025. That sentiment is upheld and shared; the shoe is Best Overall on our list of Best Running Shoes. For $150 (and frequently on sale), just above the cost of the New Balance Ellipse, you could also say it’s Best Value. And because of its secret sauce, Adidas’s Lightstrike Pro midsole, which is featured in the brand’s super shoes, you could also say it’s Best for Speedwork, too.

According to recent reports, one woman tester gamely raced in the Adizero Evo SL, and experienced excellent results. “The coolest thing about these to me was the weight and cushion,” said that tester, Caroline Lennon. “It was a perfect balance of being light and springy but still feeling well-cushioned and supported. They were so comfortable at all paces and let me feel faster than I was anticipating. They felt best at a harder effort. My 5K race was surprisingly fast given that there was no carbon plate!”.

Breaking: A Nike shoe with Hoka-plush cushioning. The Vomero 18 is unlike any Nike we’ve tested. It has a dual-density midsole with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foam, which puts this shoe in the super trainer category. What you get is a bouncy, soft ride that makes long runs an energized quest instead of a Saturday (or Sunday) morning slog.

“I didn’t expect to love this shoe as much as I do!” stated Associate Health and Fitness Editor Kristine Kearns, a self-described loyal Brooks Ghost fan. “I wasn’t sure if I would like the Vomero 18 because of how much heel cushioning there is, and how it kind of elevates me forward in that way. But it turns out the shoe provides so much stability, even on the side.”.

It has been revealed that the source of the stability Kearns is referring to: the wider platform. Nike collected input from women testers, who wanted a wider fit in the midfoot. The result is a more accommodating foot shape that provides midrun support.

Recent findings suggest that the Endorphin Elite 3 makes good with super adjustments after a strong reception with the Endorphin Elite 2. Several testers loved the previous model’s aggressive bounce, becoming inspired to race in it at their next marathon. Others, like me, had difficulty troubleshooting the squishy TPEE foam. It was volatile, pogo stick-like bounce that required mastering before you went all out on this somewhat unstable super shoe.

Sources indicate that saucony tamed the shoe this go-around. That pogo stick bounce is still there, but the ride is more stable with a connected heel and midfoot (not the slightly decoupled heel that made it more likely to turn your foot inward navigating sharp turns). The PwrTrac outsole also adds more support by providing grippy traction.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

The Adrenaline GTS 25 is pumped with even more foam for a comfier, more supportive ride. Brooks added 1 mm of DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and 3 mm in the forefoot, resulting in a slightly higher stack height, lower heel drop, and more responsive ride.

According to recent reports, dense guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to help with ankle and knee alignment while running. The support aids overpronators and late-onset overpronators alike.

“One of the shoe’s best features is the sense of security it provides,” mentioned tester Kylie Rodriguez. “The Adrenaline series is known for its stability, and this model is no exception. I felt confident and secure on every surface, from slick sidewalks to uneven dirt paths.

Sources indicate that “This blend of comfort, stability, and a lightweight feel makes the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 a fantastic and reliable choice for any runner looking for a do-it-all shoe. It’s a solid, dependable performer that won’t let you down. Another solid key component to the shoe was the cupping support the heel gave my strong heel striking steps even more confidence and support.”.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Recent findings suggest that we’re still getting in Torin 9 feedback, but it’s safe to say early on that the shoe is a worthy follow-up to the Torin 8. When Altra was founded in 2009, its core values were balanced zero-drop cushioning, an accommodating toebox for toe-splaying, and a women-specific fit. The brand has evolved with a 4mm-drop shoe line but its values haven’t changed.

The Torin, basically the Ghost version of a zero-drop shoe, is a terrific cushioned entry into running a no-drop shoe. Dual-density foam provides a moderate but supportive bed of cushioning to help you transition into zero-drop running. Runners with wide feet and bunions will also appreciate Altra’s wide toebox, which not only allows your toes to wiggle but also helps with your biomechanics (squeezed toes help you run faster, noted no one ever).

According to recent reports, the updated outsole is Vibram XS Dura, which is grippier than the rubber on the Torin 8. I like how the shoe can dabble off road and not have to worry about falling face-first when I traverse onto a trail—which is rare.

The lululemon shoe team has made it its mission to produce women-specific trainers since the release of the brand’s first running shoe, the Blissfeel, in 2022. Their latest model, the Wildfeel, provides the same comfy, secure fit with a responsive, high-rebound ride off-road.

According to recent reports, the shoe has men’s and women’s editions, which are tweaked to support each sex’s anatomical differences and distinct biomechanics. For instance, the forefoot of the women’s shoe is slightly more flexible than the men’s to complement the shorter toes, longer arch, and shorter instep typical of women’s feet.

Our testers appreciated the Wildfeel’s flexibility and overall comfort. It’s a good choice for runners fresh to the trail who want more of a hybrid option that can take on some technical track.

According to recent reports, “I loved the flexibility of the Wildfeels!” said tester Jenny Stump. “I am primarily a road runner. These felt comfortable enough that I could do some easy miles on the road as well as tackle some trails with uneven surfaces. All the trail runners I have previously tried felt more stiff and had such a thick sole that I wouldn’t even want to warm up on the road with them.”.

Industry observers note that what I love most about the Experience Wild 3 is that it’s a trail shoe that feels like a road shoe. The fit is accommodating in the midfoot and toe area—Altra is known for its spacious toeboxes that allow your toes to splay—and the collar and tongue are padded and cushioned.

The Altra Ego P35 foam is responsive on the trail and provides a nice balance of support and ground feel. Another win for me, the mostly road runner: the shoe is incredibly flexible. No stiffness or hot spots that cause my feet a world of hurt the first couple of runs before they’re broken in.

It has been revealed that the shoes have gaiter attachments to provide even more protection and a toe sweep. The drop is a low 4 mm, which isn’t as intimidating as going full zero (though if you’re game, the Lone Peak 9 is a good place to start).

The shoe is also available as the Experience Wild 3+, which has a Vibram Megagrip outsole. It’s a little more expensive at $165. If you want tackier grip, go for it. But the 3.5mm lugs on the MaxTrac outsole suit me and fellow testers just fine on slush, mud, and icy snow.

Women’s feet have distinct structural differences than men’s feet. From shape to proportions to biomechanics, all of these things significantly impact shoe fit and comfort. For example, while men’s feet typically present a more uniform width from heel to forefoot, women’s feet tend to be wider in the forefoot relative to the heel. Any lady who has felt their toes get squished as their heel slips right out of the shoe knows this matter.

Recognizing these anatomical differences, and responding to the hoards of women runners clamoring for something better, running shoe manufacturers have (finally) started to incorporate more gender-specific design elements into their products. This means crafting shoes with distinct features tailored to the unique shape and biomechanics of women’s feet. For instance, a women’s running shoe might feature a wider toebox to accommodate the broader ball of the foot, while a narrower heel counter secures the back of the foot and prevents slippage.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, the materials used in the heel construction might differ between men’s and women’s versions to account for variations in where we strike our foot when we land. Women and men obviously have different centers of gravity—especially when we’re pregnant—and that changes how we strike and the wear pattern of our soles.

In a recent development, brands are not just shrinking and pinking the shoes anymore. Their aim is to enhance performance and prevent running-related aches and pains. A shoe that fits properly and supports the foot’s natural movement can improve running efficiency and reduce the risk of common running-related injuries, such as blisters, plantar fasciitis, the pedi-ick black toenails, and shin splints.

Researchers have also found that, because women tend to have wider hips than men, women’s feet are more likely to strike the ground toward the outside of their shoe soles. The inward rolling of the foot, called pronation, that results from this explains why more women are believed to overpronate than men (aka, walk a bit duck-footed.). Some women’s running shoes account for this increased tendency with stability features in the sole, such as guide rails and medial posts, to provide more support.

This list includes what we regard as the best shoe in its category. But there are still plenty of other shoes for you to choose from.

For the plushest ride and more foam underfoot, check out the Best Cushioned Running Shoes.

If you’re an overpronator or think you need more support, take a look at the Best Stability Shoes.

And if you want more of a selection of non-road shoes, visit the Best Trail Shoes.

No matter the distance or your shoe preferences, there’s a great shoe for you on our lists.

What’s the size difference between men’s and women’s running shoes?

If you prefer wearing men’s running shoes, size down 1.5. For example: A women’s size 10 would equal a men’s size 8.5.

When should you change out your running shoes?

Sources indicate that running shoe shelf life is dependent on the runner. Some runners wear down their shoes after only a couple weeks, others have their shoes well past several months. The standard mileage on everyday trainers is 350 to 500 miles, 250 to 300 for lightweight shoes, and 100 to 250 for racing or minimalist shoes.

Industry observers note that if you don’t keep track of mileage, a good rule of thumb is switching out shoes twice a year. For racing shoes, two to three races.

How do you clean your running shoes?

You can put your shoes in the washing machine with some detergent, set on cold. Never put your shoes in the dryer—it will melt the glue and make them degrade faster.

According to recent reports, instead, remove the insoles and allow them to air dry. Stuff wads of newspaper inside your shoes and leave them to sit for a couple hours so the paper can absorb the moisture.

Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. #45281. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1754 w)
